questions.question: How does @InjectMocks injection work under the hood?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Injection Strategy | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: `@InjectMocks` is a convenience, not a dependency-injection container. Mockito first considers the largest constructor and resolves arguments from declared mocks by type; unresolved non-mockable arguments may be passed as null. If constructor injection creates the object, Mockito does not continue with setter or field injection. Otherwise it may use a no-argument instance and try property/setter injection, then field injection. Unmatched dependencies can remain null without a clear injection error, while construction failures can still throw.

sections.title: How @InjectMocks Resolves Dependencies
sections.content:
`@InjectMocks` asks Mockito to create or reuse the object under test and place declared mocks or spies into it. It is a best-effort convenience rather than a full dependency-injection container.

Mockito first considers constructor injection and chooses the largest constructor. It resolves parameters from available mocks by type; for unresolved arguments that cannot be mocked, null may be passed. If that constructor creates the object successfully, Mockito does not continue with setter or field injection.

When constructor injection is not used, Mockito can create a no-argument instance and try property/setter injection, then field injection. Matching uses type and can use field/property names to disambiguate. Some unmatched dependencies simply remain null, while an inaccessible class, inner class, interface, abstract class, or constructor exception can produce a setup error. Manual construction is clearer when wiring matters.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Constructor|~first strategy|largest constructor considered|resolve mocks by type|unresolved arguments may be null
blue|Property/setter|~next when constructor not used|two-pass type then name matching|needs usable instance|best effort
emerald|Field|~last strategy|type then name matching|reflection sets fields|unmatched fields may remain null
rose|Boundary|~not a DI container|no recursive graph|no qualifier semantics|manual construction is explicit

sections.title: Illustrating @InjectMocks Three-Phase Resolution
When to Rely on @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use **@InjectMocks** when your class has simple, single-constructor dependency injection with all dependencies as @Mock fields. It reduces boilerplate for straightforward service tests.

Avoid it when you have **multiple constructors** or **conditional initialization logic** — Mockito's silent failure will hide configuration errors. In complex scenarios (like needing different mock configurations per test), prefer **manual construction** in @BeforeEach where you explicitly call the constructor with mocks. This makes the wiring visible and fails at compile time if you pass wrong types.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Expecting an Error on Injection Failure**: Freshers assume @InjectMocks will throw an exception if a dependency can't be wired — it doesn't. It leaves the field null, causing cryptic NPE later.
- **Mixing Field and Constructor Injection**: Using @Autowired field injection in production code then wondering why @InjectMocks behaves unpredictably — the injection order becomes ambiguous.
- **Not Using @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Forgetting this annotation means @Mock and @InjectMocks aren't processed, leaving everything null and causing test failures that look like mock issues but are actually initialization problems.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- `@InjectMocks` performs best-effort injection; it is not a DI framework.
- Constructor injection considers the largest constructor and matches mocks by type.
- Unresolved constructor arguments may be null; a successful constructor stops later strategies.
- Setter/property injection and then field injection are fallback strategies.
- Manually call the constructor when you want compile-time-visible wiring.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`@InjectMocks` is a Mockito convenience for creating the class under test and injecting declared mocks or spies. It is not a replacement for Spring or another dependency-injection container.

Mockito first considers the largest constructor and resolves its arguments from available mocks by type. If a non-mockable argument cannot be resolved, Mockito may pass null. Once constructor injection creates the object, it does not continue by filling other setters and fields. When constructor injection is not used, Mockito can create a no-argument instance, try property or setter injection, and finally try field injection. Names may help when more than one mock has the same type.

Because this is best effort, an unmatched collaborator can remain null without a specific “injection failed” message. Other problems, such as a constructor throwing or a type that cannot be instantiated, can produce a setup error. For a normal service with required constructor dependencies, manually calling `new OrderService(repo, gateway)` is often the clearest and safest test wiring.

questions.question: Should you use field injection or constructor injection in production Spring services?
questions.title: Field vs Constructor Injection Spring | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit, supports final fields, and lets tests construct the class with normal Java. Field injection hides required inputs and needs the container or reflection-based test support. Spring can inject either style, but constructor injection gives an object that cannot be created without its required collaborators.

sections.title: Why Constructor Injection is the Spring Standard
sections.content:
With **constructor injection**, required collaborators are constructor parameters and can be stored in `final` fields. A caller cannot create the object without supplying them, and a unit test can use a normal `new` expression with mocks or real values.

With **field injection**, Spring sets fields after constructing the object. The required inputs are less visible in the public construction contract, the fields cannot normally be final, and a plain unit test cannot supply them through normal Java construction.

Both styles can be managed by Spring, and neither automatically solves circular design. Constructor cycles fail visibly during context creation, which is usually a useful signal to reconsider the dependency graph. For optional collaborators, a setter or explicit nullable/optional contract may be appropriate.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Constructor Injection|~The preferred style|final fields|immutable and testable|new in a plain test
blue|Field Injection|~Avoid in production|needs reflection|hidden dependencies|hard to instantiate
emerald|For Tests|~InjectMocks adapts|prefers constructor|falls back to field|matches by type

sections.title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection
When to Choose Constructor Injection
sections.content:
Use constructor parameters for collaborators that the object needs to be valid. With a single constructor, Spring does not require `@Autowired` on it.

Use setter injection only when a dependency is genuinely optional or replaceable after construction and the class has a clear valid default. Avoid field injection for new production code when the same dependency can be expressed in the constructor.

In a Spring context test, current `@MockitoBean` can override a bean regardless of whether consumers receive it through a constructor. In a plain unit test, call the constructor directly.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing Field Injection for Brevity**: Freshers pick @Autowired field injection because it's fewer lines of code, not realizing they're sacrificing testability and immutability.
- **Mixing Injection Types**: Using constructor injection for some dependencies and field injection for others creates inconsistency and confusion about which are mandatory.
- **Not Using Final Fields**: Declaring constructor-injected dependencies without final allows accidental reassignment and signals to readers that the field might change, when it shouldn't.
- **Ignoring Circular Dependencies**: Field injection can mask circular dependency issues until runtime; constructor injection surfaces them immediately during Spring context startup.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Constructor injection**: required dependencies are explicit and can be final
- **Plain tests**: create the subject with a normal constructor call
- **Single constructor**: Spring can use it without `@Autowired`
- **Field injection**: dependencies are assigned after construction and hidden from the constructor contract
- **Circular dependency**: visible startup failure is a design signal, not a reason to prefer fields

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use constructor injection for required collaborators because the constructor states what the class needs and allows those fields to be final. For example, a test can create `new OrderService(repository, gateway)` with two Mockito mocks and no Spring context; the compiler also prevents construction when one required argument is missing. Field injection lets Spring set private fields after construction, but it hides required inputs from normal object creation and leaves the object temporarily incomplete. Spring can manage both styles, yet constructor injection exposes a circular dependency clearly during context creation. A setter can still make sense for a genuinely optional or replaceable collaborator with a valid default.

questions.question: How do you manually inject mocks without using @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Manual Mock Injection Without @InjectMocks | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: Create the class under test manually in @BeforeEach, passing mocks as constructor arguments. This is explicit, debuggable, and fails loudly if arguments don't match. Preferred for complex setups where @InjectMocks silent failure would be hard to debug.

sections.title: Manual Mock Injection for Explicit Control
sections.content:
Manual mock injection means you create the test subject yourself in **@BeforeEach**, passing mocks directly as constructor arguments. You create mocks using **@Mock** annotations or **Mockito.mock()**, then instantiate your service with a plain constructor call. This approach gives you complete visibility into the wiring — no hidden Mockito resolution logic, no silent failures. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the **compiler catches it immediately**. Manual injection is especially valuable when you need **different configurations** of the same service across tests, or when the service has **conditional initialization logic** that @InjectMocks can't handle.

Think of it as choosing explicitness over convenience: a few extra lines of code in exchange for zero ambiguity and instant compile-time feedback.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Manual Wiring|~No annotation|new Service of mocks|an explicit constructor|full control
blue|Why Bother|~Clarity|obvious dependencies|no reflection magic|easy to debug
emerald|Trade-off|~More typing|update on signature change|InjectMocks is shorter|both are valid

sections.title: Manual Injection vs @InjectMocks
When Manual Injection is Better
sections.content:
Choose manual injection when your tests need **multiple configurations** of the same service — for example, testing behavior with and without an optional dependency.

Use it when the service has **complex constructors** with multiple overloads or factory methods that @InjectMocks can't resolve reliably.

Prefer manual injection in **parameterized tests** where you loop through different mock setups — creating the service inside the test method makes each iteration independent. Finally, use it when you're **new to Mockito** and want to understand exactly how your test objects are wired before relying on annotation magic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Recreating Mocks in @BeforeEach**: Freshers sometimes call Mockito.mock() inside setUp() without using @Mock annotations, losing the automatic cleanup that MockitoExtension provides.
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith**: Even when manually constructing the service, you still need MockitoExtension to process @Mock annotations — without it, all mocks are null.
- **Over-Using Manual Injection**: Writing manual setup for every test when @InjectMocks would work fine — this adds boilerplate without benefit. Use manual injection when it actually solves a problem, not as a blanket rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Explicit Wiring**: You see exactly which mock is passed to which constructor parameter — no hidden resolution
- **Compile-Time Safety**: Type mismatches and missing arguments fail at compile time, not at runtime
- **Test Isolation**: Each test can create a different configuration of the service without affecting others
- **No Silent Failures**: If a mock isn't wired, you get a compiler error or immediate NPE, not a confusing failure later
- **@Mock Still Useful**: You still use @Mock to create mocks and @ExtendWith for cleanup — manual injection only affects the service construction

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To manually inject mocks without at-InjectMocks, you create the test subject yourself in the at-BeforeEach method by calling its constructor with the mocks as arguments. First, you declare your mocks using at-Mock annotations or Mockito.mock calls. Then, in setUp, you instantiate the service with a plain constructor call, passing the mocks explicitly. For example, if I'm testing OrderService, I'd create the paymentGateway and inventoryRepo mocks, then do orderService equals new OrderService with those mocks as parameters. This approach gives you complete control and makes the wiring obvious. If you pass the wrong type or forget a dependency, the compiler catches it immediately — you don't have to wait for a runtime NPE. Manual injection is especially useful when you need different configurations of the same service across tests. Maybe one test needs the service with an email sender, another without. With manual construction, you just create two different instances in the respective test methods. It's a few extra lines of code, but you get zero ambiguity and instant feedback. I still use at-Mock annotations for creating the mocks themselves because MockitoExtension handles cleanup automatically. Manual injection only replaces the at-InjectMocks step. This pattern is common in teams that value explicitness over annotation magic.

questions.question: What is @MockBean in Spring Boot testing and how does it differ from @Mock?
questions.title: @MockBean vs @Mock Spring Boot | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: `@Mock` creates a standalone Mockito mock and does not add it to Spring. The older Spring Boot `@MockBean` replaces or adds a bean inside a test `ApplicationContext`; since Spring Boot 3.4 it is deprecated for removal in Boot 4.0 in favor of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`. Use `@Mock` for a plain unit test and a bean override when a Spring test such as `@WebMvcTest` needs the mock in context-managed wiring.

sections.title: Understanding @MockBean in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
`@Mock` is a Mockito annotation. It creates one mock object after Mockito's extension, runner, or `openMocks` initializes the test. Spring does not know about that object, so the test wires it into the class under test directly.

The older Spring Boot `@MockBean` is a test-context feature. It replaces an existing bean, or adds one when suitable, so other objects created by Spring receive the Mockito mock. Since Spring Boot 3.4, `@MockBean` is deprecated for removal in Boot 4.0; new code should use Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`. The matching spy annotation is `@MockitoSpyBean`.

A bean override is useful in a slice or application-context test, but it is not what makes a test load Spring—the surrounding annotation such as `@WebMvcTest` or `@SpringBootTest` does that. Override declarations also form part of the context-cache key, so keeping them consistent helps Spring reuse test contexts.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~Plain Mockito|no Spring context|fast unit test|the ExtendWith extension
blue|the MockBean annotation|~Spring context|replaces a bean|integration or slice|slower startup
emerald|Pick Rule|~Default to Mock|MockBean needs context|use with SpringBootTest|or WebMvcTest

sections.title: @Mock vs @MockBean in Tests
When to Use @Mock vs @MockBean
sections.content:
Use **`@Mock`** when the subject can be constructed directly. This keeps the unit test independent of Spring and makes every dependency visible in the constructor.

Use **`@MockitoBean`**—or legacy `@MockBean` on an older Boot baseline—when Spring must create the subject and inject the replacement. A common case is `@WebMvcTest`, where Spring creates the controller and the test overrides its service collaborator.

Do not replace a repository with a mock in a test whose purpose is to verify repository queries or transaction behavior. That test needs the real relevant infrastructure instead.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the wrong lifecycle**: `@Mock` needs Mockito initialization; a Spring bean override needs a Spring TestContext.
- **Confusing context loading with mocking**: `@MockBean` does not by itself turn a plain unit test into a Spring test.
- **Unnecessary context tests**: if `new OrderService(mockGateway)` is enough, a plain Mockito test is clearer.
- **Ignoring current APIs**: on current Spring versions, prefer `@MockitoBean`; `@MockBean` is the older Boot annotation.
- **Fragmenting the context cache**: inconsistent override declarations across test classes can reduce reuse of cached contexts.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@Mock`**: standalone Mockito object; Spring does not register it
- **`@MockitoBean`**: current Spring Framework annotation that overrides a bean in a test context
- **`@MockBean`**: older Spring Boot annotation, deprecated since Boot 3.4 for removal in 4.0
- **Unit test**: construct the subject directly and use `@Mock`
- **Spring slice/context test**: use a bean override only when Spring-managed wiring is part of the test

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `@Mock` creates a Mockito mock outside Spring. I use it in a unit test, construct the service myself, and pass the mock through the constructor. A Spring bean-override annotation is different: it puts the mock into the test `ApplicationContext`, so controllers or services created by Spring receive it. Older Spring Boot code calls this `@MockBean`; since Boot 3.4 that annotation is deprecated for removal in 4.0, and current code uses Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`. For example, a `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` can declare `@MockitoBean OrderService service` because Spring creates the controller. A plain `OrderService` test normally needs only `@Mock PaymentGateway` and direct constructor wiring. Different bean overrides can also create different context-cache keys, so I keep them consistent rather than claiming that each annotation simply invalidates the whole cache.

questions.question: What happens when @InjectMocks cannot inject a mock?
questions.title: @InjectMocks Silent Injection Failure
questions.direct_answer: `@InjectMocks` can leave a collaborator null when no declared mock or spy matches it, because Mockito does not report every unsatisfied injection point as an error. The failure often appears later when the test executes that path. However, not every injection problem is silent: Mockito can fail setup if it cannot instantiate the target or its constructor throws. Strict stubbing does not validate injection; it reports unused or mismatched stubs.

sections.title: Silent Failure Mode of @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Mockito's injection is best effort. If a field or setter has no matching mock or spy, that collaborator may remain null and the test may fail only when the code uses it. This is the “silent” part: Mockito does not promise to report every unsatisfied dependency.

There are visible failures too. Mockito may report that it cannot instantiate an interface, abstract class, non-static inner class, or class without a usable constructor, and it can surface an exception thrown by the chosen constructor.

`STRICT_STUBS` solves a different problem. It can report unnecessary stubbing and some argument mismatches; it does not prove that `@InjectMocks` wired every collaborator. Prefer required constructor dependencies and explicit `new` construction when missing wiring should be obvious.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Silent Failure|~No error thrown|the field stays null|the test NPEs later|hard to debug
blue|Why It Happens|~No match found|a type mismatch|a name mismatch|a missing Mock field
emerald|The Fix|~Make it explicit|check the Mock is declared|prefer constructor|or wire manually

sections.title: Silent Injection Failure Example
How to Avoid Silent Injection Failures
sections.content:
Use `@InjectMocks` when the subject has simple, unambiguous dependencies and the inferred wiring is easy to understand.

Use direct constructor construction when dependencies are required, when several collaborators share a type, or when a test needs deliberately different arrangements. A normal `new Service(repo, gateway)` exposes missing and reordered parameters at compile time.

Mockito strictness validates stubbing quality; it does not validate dependency completeness. If the test uses annotation fields, initialize them with `MockitoExtension`, a runner, or the `openMocks` lifecycle.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Trusting @InjectMocks to Fail Loudly**: Freshers assume any issue with dependency wiring will throw an exception during test setup. It doesn't — you get an NPE during test execution instead.
- **Typos in Mock Field Names**: Declaring a mock with a typo like auditLoger when the class field is auditLogger. Mockito can't match by name, so it leaves the field null.
- **Not Using @ExtendWith**: Forgetting @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) means Mockito doesn't process annotations, so all @Mock and @InjectMocks fields are null. The error looks like an injection failure but is actually a setup failure.
- **Ignoring Constructor Injection**: Continuing to use field injection in production code because it's familiar, not realizing constructor injection would prevent all these silent test failures.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- An unmatched mock candidate can leave a dependency null without a dedicated injection error.
- Instantiation and constructor failures can still fail test setup.
- Strict stubbing checks stubs, not dependency completeness.
- Required constructor dependencies reduce partially initialized objects.
- Manual construction is the most explicit test wiring.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
When `@InjectMocks` cannot match a declared mock or spy to one dependency, Mockito may leave that collaborator null instead of reporting an unsatisfied injection point. The test then fails later only if execution reaches code that uses the field.

That does not mean every problem is silent. Mockito can fail setup when the target is an interface, abstract class, non-static inner class, or otherwise cannot be instantiated. A constructor that throws can also produce a setup error.

Strict stubbing does not validate the injection graph. It reports unnecessary stubs and certain stubbing mismatches, so an unused stub may be a clue but not proof. Required constructor dependencies make invalid objects harder to create, and explicit test construction—`service = new Service(repo, gateway)`—makes missing arguments visible to the compiler.

questions.question: How does Mockito decide between constructor injection and field injection for @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Constructor vs Field Injection in @InjectMocks
questions.direct_answer: For `@InjectMocks`, Mockito considers constructor injection first and chooses the largest constructor, resolving mock arguments by type and possibly passing null for unresolved non-mockable parameters. If construction succeeds, it stops there. Otherwise it can try property/setter injection and then field injection on a usable instance. In production code, required constructor injection is usually clearer because callers must supply dependencies and tests can instantiate the class explicitly.

sections.title: Mockito's Three-Phase Injection Strategy
sections.content:
Mockito's first `@InjectMocks` strategy is constructor injection. It considers the largest constructor and resolves parameters from available mocks by type. Missing non-mockable values may become null. If the object is created through that constructor, Mockito does not continue with setter or field injection.

If constructor injection is not used, Mockito can create or reuse an instance and try setters/properties, then fields. Type is the main match, with names used to resolve some ambiguity.

For production design, constructor injection is useful because required dependencies are visible and can be stored in final fields. Tests can bypass Mockito's injection rules and call the constructor directly. Field injection hides requirements and creates partially initialized objects more easily.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Decision Order|~Mockito picks one|biggest constructor first|then property setters|then fields
blue|Constructor Path|~The preferred path|matches args by type|all-or-nothing|cleanest result
emerald|Fallback|~If no constructor|setter injection|then field reflection|name breaks ties

sections.title: Injection Order in Action
Choosing the Right Injection Strategy
sections.content:
Use **constructor injection** for all mandatory dependencies in production code — it aligns with Mockito's first phase and makes dependencies explicit. Mockito picks the largest constructor it can satisfy, so if you have multiple constructors, the one with the most parameters matching @Mock types wins.

Use **setter injection** only for truly optional dependencies that have sensible defaults. Mockito calls matching setters after constructor injection completes.

Avoid relying on **field injection** in production code — while Mockito can handle it as a fallback, it bypasses encapsulation and offers no compile-time validation. If you find yourself needing precise control over which mocks go where, skip @InjectMocks and use manual construction in @BeforeEach.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming Field Injection is First**: Freshers think Mockito directly assigns mocks to fields because that's what Spring does with @Autowired field injection. Mockito actually tries constructors first.
- **Multiple Constructors Without Clarity**: Having several constructors without understanding that Mockito picks the largest one that matches available mocks, which can inject unintended configurations.
- **Mixing Injection Styles Randomly**: Using constructor injection for some dependencies and field injection for others without a clear pattern, making tests unpredictable.
- **Not Marking Optional Dependencies**: Declaring all dependencies as constructor parameters, even optional ones, forcing test setup to provide mocks for features not relevant to the test.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Constructor injection is considered before setter and field strategies.
- The largest constructor is selected; unresolved arguments can become null.
- Successful constructor injection stops later strategies.
- Setter and field matching are best effort by type and sometimes name.
- Prefer explicit constructor dependencies for production design and simple tests.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
With `@InjectMocks`, Mockito first considers constructor injection. It selects the largest constructor and tries to resolve arguments from the mocks and spies declared in the test. An unresolved non-mockable argument may be passed as null. If the constructor successfully creates the object, Mockito does not then fill remaining setters or fields.

When constructor injection is not used, Mockito can try property or setter injection and finally field injection. These strategies mainly match by type and may use names when types are ambiguous.

I prefer required constructor injection in production code because it makes dependencies part of the class contract and allows final fields. In a unit test I can write `new OrderService(orderRepository, paymentGateway)`, so the compiler checks the wiring. That design benefit is more important than relying on Mockito's strategy order.

questions.question: How do you test a class that uses constructor injection without @InjectMocks?
questions.title: Manual Constructor Injection in Tests
questions.direct_answer: Create the mocks with @Mock or Mockito.mock(), then pass them directly to the class constructor in @BeforeEach — no @InjectMocks needed, and the wiring is explicit and compile-time checked.

sections.title: Testing Constructor-Injected Classes Without @InjectMocks
sections.content:
When your production class uses **constructor injection**, testing it without @InjectMocks is straightforward and explicit. You create mocks using **@Mock annotations** (processed by MockitoExtension) or **Mockito.mock()** calls, then in your **@BeforeEach** method, you instantiate the test subject by calling its constructor directly with the mocks as arguments.

This approach is **self-documenting**: anyone reading the test sees exactly which mock goes to which constructor parameter. It's **compile-time safe**: if you pass the wrong type or forget an argument, the code won't compile. It eliminates the **silent failure risk** of @InjectMocks, where injection failures leave fields null and cause NPE at runtime. Many teams prefer this explicit style because it removes a layer of annotation magic and makes tests easier to debug when something goes wrong.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Constructor Injection|~Easiest to test|just call new|pass the mocks in|no framework needed
blue|With InjectMocks|~Auto constructor|matches by type|the extension wires it|less boilerplate
emerald|Best Practice|~Plain new is clear|explicit and simple|InjectMocks for many deps|both are fine

sections.title: Explicit Constructor Injection in Tests
When to Choose Explicit Over @InjectMocks
sections.content:
Use explicit constructor calls when you have **complex test scenarios** that need different configurations of the same service — just create multiple instances in individual test methods with different mock setups.

Prefer explicit construction when you're new to Mockito and want to **understand the wiring** before relying on annotations.

Use it when your class has **multiple constructors** and you want to test each one separately — @InjectMocks picks the largest matching constructor automatically, but explicit calls let you choose. Finally, use explicit construction in **parameterized tests** or **test factories** where you generate test subjects programmatically.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting @ExtendWith**: Even when manually constructing the service, you still need @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to process @Mock annotations. Without it, all mocks are null.
- **Creating New Mocks in setUp**: Calling Mockito.mock() inside @BeforeEach without using @Mock annotations loses the automatic cleanup and reset that MockitoExtension provides between tests.
- **Over-Engineering Simple Tests**: Using explicit construction for every single test when @InjectMocks would work fine, adding unnecessary boilerplate. Use explicit construction when it solves a real problem, not as dogma.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Explicit Wiring**: Constructor call shows exactly which mock is passed to which parameter — zero ambiguity
- **Compile-Time Safety**: Type mismatches, wrong argument order, or missing arguments fail at compile time
- **No Silent Failures**: If a dependency isn't provided, the compiler catches it immediately, not at runtime with NPE
- **@Mock Still Useful**: Continue using @Mock annotations for creating mocks — MockitoExtension handles initialization and cleanup
- **Flexible Configuration**: Easy to create different service configurations per test by calling the constructor with different arguments

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To test a class with constructor injection without using at-InjectMocks, you just create the test subject manually by calling its constructor. First, you declare your mocks using at-Mock annotations or Mockito.mock calls. Then, in the at-BeforeEach method, you instantiate the service by calling its constructor and passing the mocks as arguments. For example, if OrderService has a constructor that takes PaymentGateway and InventoryRepository, you'd write orderService equals new OrderService with paymentGateway and inventoryRepo as parameters. The advantage is that this wiring is completely explicit. Anyone reading the test can see exactly which mock goes where. If you pass the wrong type or forget an argument, the compiler catches it immediately — you don't have to wait for a runtime error. This approach eliminates the silent failure problem with at-InjectMocks, where injection fails but you only discover it when the test throws a NullPointerException. You still use at-Mock annotations to create the mocks because MockitoExtension handles initialization and cleanup automatically. The manual construction only replaces the at-InjectMocks step. I find this pattern especially useful when I need different configurations of the same service across tests. Instead of relying on at-InjectMocks to figure out the wiring, I just create the service with the exact mocks I need for each test. It's a few extra lines of code, but it makes the test self-documenting and much easier to debug.
